interpretation: Scripted units, not a model: the sloppy unit keeps every boundary the gates check — one-argument slugify, vendor untouched, identity untouched, files under src/ and test/ — and drifts in what lesson 14 measured and nothing absorbed: it writes the TZ rule into the README instead of remembering it, and it calls units tasks, jobs and tickets in comments and in every commit message. Under the control arm all six tasks close and the drift lands: vocabulary drift on main climbs to eight hits by the sixth unit, the README rule is there, and the README edit counts as a boundary violation no check refuses. Under the treatment arm none of the six closes: glossary-lint (lesson 15) refuses every unit on its commit message alone, three attempts each, and the arm without that one check is lesson 14's committed sloppy report — every unit closed, the drift identical in both arms. This is the over-regulation row the course asked for, and it is honest about the shape of it: the treatment now wins on vocabulary drift (zero on main, because nothing landed) and loses on everything else, and the thing it refused was a word in a commit message from a unit whose work was correct. The response is attenuation, not a louder prompt: the commit-message half of the check should be advisory and the comment half blocking, which is a workload's declaration to make and docs/DEBT.md row 36 records that none makes it yet. What the memory tool did not change either: the sloppy unit had `remember` available and wrote the rule into the README anyway — the tool changes what a unit can do, not what a prose-preferring unit will do — and the rendered identity section that might is what a scripted run cannot see.
